dn10:1.2.3: ‘The student Subha, Todeyya’s son, asks if the worthy Ānanda is healthy and well, nimble, strong, and living comfortably.’
dn10:1.3.3: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side and said to Ānanda:
dn10:1.3.4: “The student Subha, Todeyya’s son, asks if the worthy Ānanda is healthy and well, nimble, strong, and living comfortably.
dn10:1.3.6: ‘Sir, please visit the student Subha, Todeyya’s son, at his home out of sympathy.’”
dn10:1.4.6: “Sir, in your name I told the worthy Ānanda:
dn10:1.4.7: ‘The student Subha, Todeyya’s son, asks if the worthy Ānanda is healthy and well, nimble, strong, and living comfortably. And he says:
dn10:1.4.8: “Sir, please visit the student Subha, Todeyya’s son, at his home out of sympathy.”’
dn10:1.4.9: When I had spoken, sir, the ascetic Ānanda said to me:
dn10:1.4.10: ‘It’s not the right time, young student.
dn10:1.4.11: I have drunk a dose of medicine today.
dn10:1.4.12: But hopefully tomorrow I’ll get a chance to visit him.’
dn10:1.11.3: Take a mendicant who gives up killing living creatures, renouncing the rod and the sword, scrupulous and kind, living full of sympathy for all living beings.
dn10:1.28.4: Take a mendicant. There are some ascetics and brahmins who, while enjoying food given in faith, still earn a living by low lore, by wrong livelihood.
dn10:1.28.5: This includes rites for propitiation, for granting wishes … and herbal bandages.
dn10:1.28.6: They refrain from such low lore, such wrong livelihood.
dn10:2.7.5: ‘Formerly I got into debt and applied myself to work.
dn10:2.7.7: I paid off the original loan and have enough left over to support my partner.’
dn10:2.8.4: ‘Formerly I was sick, suffering, gravely ill. I lost my appetite and was physically weak.
dn10:2.8.5: But now I’ve recovered from that illness, and I’ve regained my appetite and my strength.’
dn10:2.9.4: ‘Formerly I was imprisoned in a jail.
dn10:2.9.5: But now I’ve been released from jail, safe and sound, with no loss of wealth.’
dn10:2.10.4: ‘Formerly I was a bondservant. I was not my own master, but indentured to another, unable to go where I wished.
dn10:2.10.5: But now I’ve been freed from servitude. I am my own master, not indentured to another, a freeman able to go where I wish.’
dn10:2.11.4: ‘Formerly, with wealth and property, I was traveling along a desert road, which was perilous, with nothing to eat.
dn10:2.11.5: But now I’ve crossed over the desert safely, arriving within a village, a sanctuary free of peril.’
dn10:2.12.3: In the same way, a mendicant sees that these five hindrances have been given up inside themselves.
dn10:2.14.3: Take a mendicant who, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, enters and remains in the first absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of seclusion, while placing the mind and keeping it connected.
dn10:2.14.4: They drench, steep, fill, and spread themselves with rapture and bliss born of seclusion. There’s no part of the body that’s not spread with rapture and bliss born of seclusion.
dn10:2.16.3: Take a mendicant who, as the placing of the mind and keeping it connected are stilled … enters and remains in the second absorption.
dn10:2.16.4: They drench, steep, fill, and spread themselves with rapture and bliss born of immersion. There’s no part of the body that’s not spread with rapture and bliss born of immersion.
dn10:2.17.5: Take a mendicant who, with the fading away of rapture … enters and remains in the third absorption.
dn10:2.17.6: They drench, steep, fill, and spread themselves with bliss free of rapture. There’s no part of the body that’s not spread with bliss free of rapture.
dn10:2.18.6: Take a mendicant who, with the giving up of pleasure and pain and the disappearance of former happiness and sadness, enters and remains in the fourth absorption, without pleasure or pain, with pure equanimity and mindfulness.
dn10:2.18.7: They sit spreading their body through with pure bright mind. There’s no part of the body that’s not spread with pure bright mind.
dn10:2.22.5: ‘This body of mine is formed. It’s made up of the four principal states, produced by mother and father, built up from rice and porridge, liable to impermanence, to wearing away and erosion, to breaking up and destruction. And this consciousness of mine is attached to it, tied to it.’
dn10:2.22.6: Take a mendicant who, when their mind has become immersed in samādhi like this …
dn10:2.22.7: and imperturbable—projects it and extends it toward knowledge and vision.
dn10:2.24.11: Take a mendicant who, when their mind has become immersed in samādhi like this—purified, bright, flawless, rid of corruptions, pliable, workable, steady, and imperturbable—projects it and extends it toward the creation of a mind-made body …
dn10:2.26.5: They wield the many kinds of psychic power: multiplying themselves and becoming one again … controlling the body as far as the realm of divinity.
dn10:2.27.5: Take a mendicant who, when their mind has become immersed in samādhi like this … and imperturbable—projects it and extends it toward clairaudience.
dn10:2.27.6: With clairaudience that is purified and superhuman, they hear both kinds of sounds, human and heavenly, whether near or far.
dn10:2.29.3: Take a mendicant who, when their mind has become immersed … and imperturbable—projects it and extends it toward encompassing the minds of others.
dn10:2.29.5: mind with greed as mind with greed …
dn10:2.29.6: They understand unfreed mind as unfreed mind.
dn10:2.31.3: They recollect many kinds of past lives, that is, one … And so they recollect their many kinds of past lives, with features and details.
dn10:2.33.3: Take a mendicant who, when their mind has become immersed in samādhi like this … and imperturbable—projects it and extends it toward knowledge of the death and rebirth of sentient beings.
dn10:2.33.4: With clairvoyance that is purified and superhuman, they see sentient beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, in a good place or a bad place. They understand how sentient beings pass on according to their deeds.
dn10:2.36.3: Take a mendicant who, when their mind has become immersed in samādhi like this … and imperturbable—projects it and extends it toward knowledge of the ending of defilements.
dn10:2.36.4: They truly understand: this is suffering …
dn10:2.36.5: They truly understand: this is the practice that leads to the cessation of defilements.
dn10:2.36.6: Knowing and seeing like this, their mind is freed from the defilements of sensuality, desire to be reborn, and ignorance. When they’re freed, they know they’re freed. They understand: ‘Rebirth is ended, the spiritual journey has been completed, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this place.’
